title: World War II
objective: After this level you can explain how the US fought and won World War II in Europe and the Pacific, from D-Day to Japan's surrender.
summary: The US fought across two oceans, from Midway and D-Day to the atomic bombs and Japan's surrender in 1945, a decision historians still debate.

cards.headline: The US military grew from about 334,000 in 1939 to over 12 million in 1945.
cards.body: It needed them: this war was fought across two oceans at once. How did the US help win it, and why do historians still argue about how it ended?

cards.headline: Midway turns the Pacific
cards.body: At Midway, from June 4 to 7, 1942, US code breakers uncovered Japan's plan. Japan lost four aircraft carriers, and the Pacific war turned in America's favor.

cards.headline: D-Day
cards.body: On June 6, 1944, nearly 160,000 Allied troops landed in Normandy, France. Americans came ashore at Utah and Omaha beaches. Less than a year later, in May 1945, Germany surrendered.

cards.headline: A code no one could crack
cards.body: The Marines trained over 400 Navajo men as Code Talkers, many serving in the Pacific. They passed messages in their own language, and the Japanese never broke their code.

cards.headline: The bomb and the argument
cards.body: The US dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on August 6 and Nagasaki on August 9, 1945. The next day Japan's emperor pushed to surrender, and Japan formally surrendered on September 2, 1945. Traditionalist historians argue the bombs were necessary to save American lives and prevent an invasion. Revisionists such as Gar Alperovitz argue they were unnecessary since Japan was near surrender, and partly aimed at the Soviets.

mascot.line: The facts of August 1945 aren't in dispute. The argument is over why, and whether it was necessary. Know both cases.

cards.headline: World War II: explained
learned: Midway turned the Pacific war in 1942
D-Day opened the way to Germany's surrender in 1945
Navajo Code Talkers sent messages no one could break
Historians still debate the atomic bombings
